The costs, benefits, and geography of environmental decisions.

Google Scholar ↗ORCID ↗

About

I study how the costs and benefits of environmental investments vary across places and people, and how this evidence can inform better resource allocation. My work connects environmental economics and spatial analysis across urban green space, energy systems, and land use.

My current research focuses on urban trees and heat adaptation in Global South cities. I assess human heat exposure, lifecycle carbon impacts, and financial costs to guide where and how urban greening investments should be made.

I received my PhD from Renmin University of China in 2024. As a Visiting PhD Researcher at Duke University’s Nicholas School of the Environment (2022–2023), I worked with Prof. Dalia Patino-Echeverri on energy and environmental research, a collaboration that continues today.

Research

My projects examine how the location of environmental decisions affects their effectiveness, costs, and distributional consequences.

01

Urban trees &
heat adaptation

Evaluating the heat-exposure reductions, lifecycle carbon impacts, and costs of urban trees, and optimizing investment locations for heat adaptation in Global South cities.

02

Waste heat &
energy access

Identifying where industrial and energy-sector waste heat can supply affordable, low-carbon residential heating through spatial matching, cost–benefit analysis, and infrastructure optimization.

03

Land allocation &
governance

Examining how land allocation, governance, and interactions between cities shape environmental outcomes and the spatial distribution of development.
